title: Joshua Lim
text:
I’m a Ph.D. student in the Department of Statistical Science at Duke University, working with Jerry Reiter and Fan Li.
My research sits where causal inference meets missing data. Most methods for asking “did this treatment help, and for whom?” quietly assume you know who was treated. Often you don’t — an exposure that was never logged, a hazard recorded for only part of a population, a survey nobody answered. I build Bayesian methods that estimate heterogeneous effects anyway, and that carry the uncertainty about who was treated all the way through to the final intervals.
Before Duke I graduated summa cum laude from UCLA in 2024 with a B.S. in Applied Mathematics, Statistics and Data Science. Alongside my methods work I collaborate as a biostatistician with Duke Radiology, UC San Diego’s Moores Cancer Center, and previously Stanford Medicine — which keeps me honest about what messy, real clinical data actually looks like.
I also care a great deal about teaching: in Summer 2026 I was instructor of record for STA 199: Introduction to Data Science and Statistical Thinking.
Outside the department you’ll find me on the court with Duke Men’s Club Volleyball, performing with Duke Chinese Dance, flipping with Duke Gymnastics, or loudly defending UCLA sports deep in ACC country.

title: Research
text:
Some ICU patients receive a right-heart catheter and some don’t. Did it help — and for whom? The quantity of interest is the heterogeneous treatment effect,
\[\tau(x) = \mathbb{E}\big[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X = x\big],\]
the causal effect for different kinds of patients rather than one population average. Estimating it normally requires knowing each unit’s treatment assignment. In practice that assignment is often partly missing: a health hazard recorded only for a subpopulation, an ad exposure that was never logged, a survey item nobody answered.
Standard practice splits the problem in two — impute the missing treatments, then estimate effects — which throws away the outcome’s information about who was likely treated and understates uncertainty in the result.
Gibbs-OMIT does both at once. A single Gibbs sampler alternates between fitting a flexible tree model (Bayesian Additive Regression Trees) for \(\tau(x)\), and re-imputing who was treated using the outcome as evidence.

The result is one posterior over both the effects and the missing treatments, so uncertainty about who was treated propagates into the final intervals rather than disappearing.

In simulation the method matches an oracle that observes every treatment (MSE 2.33 vs. 2.43), a 67% reduction against complete-case analysis (7.04), while MICE does worse than simply dropping incomplete rows (9.69). Interval coverage is 95%, against 79% for complete case and 88% for MICE.

title: Research
text:
Positions

Research Assistant May 2025 – present Duke University, Department of Statistical Science
Developing causal inference methodology and applications under Jerry Reiter and Fan Li, including work on integrating LLMs and modern ML into causal discovery.


Biostatistician Dec 2025 – present UC San Diego School of Medicine, Moores Cancer Center
Statistical modeling comparing treatment-related complications between patients receiving immunotherapy with radiation versus concurrent chemoradiation with cisplatin.


Biostatistician May 2025 – present Duke University School of Medicine, Department of Radiology
Investigating how contrast density and image acquisition timing affect CSF-venous fistula visibility, using ordinal regression and related methods to support neuroradiology research.


Biostatistician and Data Manager Jun 2024 – Mar 2025 Stanford School of Medicine, Pulmonary, Allergy and Critical Care Medicine
Identified environmental factors driving asthma and COPD emergency visits and hospitalizations, tracking regional and county-wide differences with attention to vulnerable populations.


Undergraduate Researcher Feb 2023 – Jun 2024 Qing Zhou Research Group, UCLA
Structure learning of causal DAGs. Extended the CML algorithm with conditional independence tests and other procedures for discrete data, validated through simulation studies on the Hoffman2 cluster. Implemented in R, Rcpp, and RcppArmadillo.


Biostatistics Researcher Jun 2022 – May 2023 Stanford School of Medicine, Sean N. Parker Center for Allergy and Asthma Research
Analyzed patients with chronic GI symptoms in oral immunotherapy clinical trials, built ML models to harmonize allergic reaction grading scales, and developed an R Shiny application for enrollment, demographic, and forecast data used in NIH reporting.
